---
title: "4. EC2: Virtual Servers"
description: "Renting the Lemonade web servers: AMIs, instance types, key pairs, security groups, user data, EBS disks, Elastic IPs, and stop versus terminate."
---

## The problem

The network from lesson 3 is ready, but it is empty. The Lemonade Stand needs two web servers, `web1` in `eu-west-2a` and `web2` in `eu-west-2b`. Each runs nginx in front of the app on port `8080`. They should set themselves up without anyone logging in, and cost nothing on days we switch them off.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip title="Ordering a computer from a menu"}
Renting a server on EC2 is like ordering at a café. You choose:

- the **recipe**: what is already on the computer's disk when it starts, like a cake-mix box (the AMI);
- the **size**: nano, micro, small, medium, large, just like T-shirt sizes (the instance type);
- a **key** for the door (a key pair), and a **door guard** who decides who may knock (a security group);
- a **note for the first morning**: "when you wake up, install nginx and put up the menu" (user data).

**Stop** puts the computer to sleep. You stop paying for the computer, but its disk is kept, and that disk still costs a little. **Terminate** gives it back to the café forever.

Werner Vogels' fourth AWS lesson is *automation is key*: people should not have to log in and click things to set up a server ([2016](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2016/03/10-lessons-from-10-years-of-aws.html)). The note for the first morning is exactly that kind of automation.
:::

## The concept, precisely

- An **instance** is a virtual server running on AWS hardware.
- An **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image) is the starting disk: an operating system plus anything pre-installed. The Lemonade servers use **Amazon Linux 2023**. AWS publishes the newest AMI ID as a public parameter, so you never need to copy IDs by hand.
- The **instance type** sets the CPU and memory. Its name reads *family, generation, extra letters, dot, size*:

  | Name | Family | Generation | Extra letters | Size |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `t3.micro` | `t`: burstable general purpose | 3 | none | micro |
  | `t4g.micro` | `t` | 4 | `g`: AWS Graviton (ARM) | micro |
  | `m7i.large` | `m`: general purpose | 7 | `i`: Intel | large |

  Other family letters: `c` for compute-heavy work, `r` for lots of memory, `g` for GPUs. **Burstable** (`t`) instances run at a low baseline and can burst higher for short periods, which suits a small web page.

- A **key pair** lets you log in with SSH. The private key is downloaded once, and AWS keeps only the public half. **Session Manager** (part of AWS Systems Manager) lets you open a shell without SSH or open ports.
- **User data** is a script that cloud-init runs **once, as root, on the first boot**.
- **EBS** (Elastic Block Store) volumes are network disks. The root volume survives stop and start. By default it is **deleted on terminate**.
- An **Elastic IP** is a public IPv4 address that stays the same across stop and start. Every public IPv4 address costs \$0.005 per hour.
- An **instance profile** attaches an IAM role (lesson 2) to the server, so programs on it get temporary credentials instead of stored keys.
- **Instance states**: `pending → running → stopping → stopped → pending …`; terminate goes `shutting-down → terminated` and cannot be undone.

| Command or option | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aws ec2 run-instances` | starts new instances | the five essentials below | `run-instances --count 2 ...` |
| `--image-id` | which AMI | look it up, do not hard-code | `--image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64` |
| `--instance-type` | size | start small; resize later | `--instance-type t3.micro` |
| `--subnet-id` | which subnet, and therefore which AZ | private subnet for web servers | `--subnet-id subnet-...` |
| `--security-group-ids` | which door guards | one or more SG IDs | `--security-group-ids sg-...` |
| `--user-data` | first-boot script | `file://` reads a local file; 16 KB limit | `--user-data file://user-data.sh` |
| `--key-name` | SSH key pair | optional if you use Session Manager | `--key-name lemonade-key` |
| `--iam-instance-profile` | role for programs on the server | never store access keys on a server | `--iam-instance-profile Name=lemonade-web` |
| `--tag-specifications` | name and tags at launch | always set `Name` and `Project` | `'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=lemonade-web}]'` |
| `--metadata-options` | instance metadata settings | require IMDSv2 tokens | `HttpTokens=required` |
| `aws ec2 describe-instances` | lists instances | filter by tag | `--filters Name=tag:Name,Values=lemonade-web` |
| `aws ec2 stop-instances` / `start-instances` | sleep / wake | stopped: no compute charge, disk still billed | `--instance-ids i-...` |
| `aws ec2 terminate-instances` | delete forever | check the ID twice | `--instance-ids i-...` |
| `aws ec2 create-key-pair` | makes an SSH key | save the private key with `chmod 400` | `--key-name lemonade-key --query KeyMaterial` |
| `aws ec2 allocate-address` / `associate-address` | Elastic IP | release it when no longer needed | `--instance-id i-... --allocation-id eipalloc-...` |

## Worked example: two web servers that set themselves up

The first-boot note, [`examples/user-data.sh`](examples/user-data.sh):

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Runs once, as root, on the first boot of a Lemonade web server (Amazon Linux 2023).
dnf install -y nginx
echo '<h1>Lemonade Stand</h1><p>Classic lemonade: $2.50</p>' > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
systemctl enable --now nginx
```

Launch two servers with it, then list them:

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances --count 2 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 \
  --subnet-id "$PRIV" --security-group-ids "$SG" --user-data file://user-data.sh \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=lemonade-web}]' \
  --query 'Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name,PrivateIpAddress]' --output text
```

Output (LocalStack; LocalStack takes a plain AMI ID instead of `resolve:ssm:`):

```text
i-e309deca737f6ef78	t3.micro	pending	10.0.11.4
i-cf3da684e71a54fd7	t3.micro	pending	10.0.11.5
```

Both start as `pending` and get private addresses from the subnet `10.0.11.0/24`. A real launch puts `web2` in the second private subnet, `10.0.12.0/24`, so the two servers sit in different AZs. Put them to sleep, then give them back:

```bash
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-e309deca737f6ef78 i-cf3da684e71a54fd7
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-e309deca737f6ef78 i-cf3da684e71a54fd7
```

Output (LocalStack, filtered):

```text
i-e309deca737f6ef78	running	stopping
i-cf3da684e71a54fd7	running	stopping
i-e309deca737f6ef78	shutting-down
i-cf3da684e71a54fd7	shutting-down
```

## Rules and conventions

- **Servers are cattle, not pets.** Anything you set up by hand will be lost when the server is replaced. Put it in user data, or later in Ansible (Part 1) or Terraform (Part 6).
- **Look AMIs up by parameter** (`resolve:ssm:...`), because AMI IDs differ per region and change with every update.
- **Use Session Manager instead of opening port 22.** If you must use SSH, allow only your own IP.
- **Give servers a role, never access keys.**
- **Require IMDSv2** (`HttpTokens=required`) so a bug in the web app cannot easily leak the server's credentials.
- **Stop** what you will need again; **terminate** what you will not. Release unused Elastic IPs.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User data without `#!/bin/bash` on the first line | nothing gets installed | the shebang tells cloud-init how to run it; check `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log` |
| Expecting user data to run on every boot | changes made in user data never re-apply | it runs once; build a new instance or use a configuration tool |
| Lost the private key file | cannot SSH in | AWS cannot recover it; use Session Manager or replace the instance |
| Data written to the root disk, then terminate | the data is gone | keep data in RDS or S3, or set `DeleteOnTermination=false` on a data volume |
| Stopped instance "costs nothing" | small charges continue | EBS disks and Elastic IPs are billed while stopped |

## Mathematical Abstraction

Inside one family, each size step **doubles** the price (and here also the memory):

$$
r_k = r_0 \cdot 2^{k}
$$

where:

- $k$ counts size steps above the smallest size: nano $= 0$, micro $= 1$, small $= 2$, medium $= 3$, large $= 4$;
- $r_0$ is the hourly price of the smallest size, in dollars per hour;
- $r_k$ is the hourly price $k$ steps up.

Example: for `t3` in London, $r_0 = \$0.0059$ (`t3.nano`). Then `t3.large` is $r_4 = 0.0059 \times 2^4 = 0.0059 \times 16 = \$0.0944$ per hour, exactly the published price. Memory follows the same rule, $0.5 \times 2^4 = 8$ GiB. The pattern holds for these sizes. CPU does not always follow it: every size from nano to large has 2 vCPUs. So check the table before relying on it.

What a server costs in a month depends on its state:

$$
C(\text{state}) =
\begin{cases}
r \cdot h + s \cdot g & \text{running} \\
s \cdot g & \text{stopped} \\
0 & \text{terminated}
\end{cases}
$$

where:

- $C$ is the monthly cost in dollars;
- $r$ is the hourly instance price and $h$ the hours it runs;
- $s$ is the disk price in dollars per GB-month (gp3 in London: \$0.0928);
- $g$ is the disk size in GB;
- the cases say: running pays for the computer and the disk; stopped pays only for the disk; terminated pays nothing.

Example: `web1` (`t3.micro`, 8 GB gp3 disk) running all month costs $0.0118 \times 730 + 0.0928 \times 8 = 8.614 + 0.742 = \$9.36$. Stopped all month it costs $0.0928 \times 8 = \$0.74$. Terminated, \$0. If it also had a public IPv4 address, add $0.005 \times 730 = \$3.65$ in every state except terminated (prices at time of writing, November 2026).
